Parts of the Atom: Atoms are the basic building blocks of matter. An atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus that contains protons and neutrons, and electrons that move around the nucleus in a large space. A proton has a charge of +1, an electron -1 and a neutron has no charge. Protons and neutrons have nearly the same mass and electrons have very little mass. In a neutral atom the number of protons equals the number of electrons. Most of the atom is empty space. The model of the atom changed as new experiments gave new evidence, from Dalton to Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr.
Atomic Number, Mass Number and Isotopes: The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons and identifies the element. The mass number (A) is the number of protons plus neutrons. The number of neutrons is N = A - Z. In a neutral atom electrons equal protons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, so they have the same atomic number but different mass numbers, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14. An ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons: losing electrons gives a positive ion and gaining electrons gives a negative ion. The atomic mass shown on the periodic table is a weighted average of isotope masses.
Electron Arrangement: Electrons occupy energy levels (shells) around the nucleus. The first shell holds at most 2 electrons, the second shell at most 8 and the third shell at most 8 for the first 20 elements. Electrons fill the lowest shell first. The electrons in the outermost shell are valence electrons, and they determine chemical behavior. For example sodium (11 electrons) is 2, 8, 1 and has 1 valence electron; oxygen (8 electrons) is 2, 6 and has 6. An atom with a full outer shell is very stable, which is why the noble gases are unreactive. Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach a full outer shell.
The Periodic Table: The periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing atomic number. Rows are called periods and columns are called groups or families. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of valence electrons. The period number tells how many shells contain electrons. Most elements are metals on the left and in the center; nonmetals are on the right; metalloids lie along the staircase line between them and have properties of both. Mendeleev arranged the first widely accepted table in 1869 and predicted undiscovered elements. Each element has a symbol of one or two letters, such as Na for sodium and Fe for iron.
Periodic Families and Trends: Groups have family names. Group 1 are the alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium): soft, very reactive metals with 1 valence electron that form 1+ ions. Group 2 are the alkaline earth metals with 2 valence electrons. Group 17 are the halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine): very reactive nonmetals with 7 valence electrons that form 1- ions. Group 18 are the noble gases (helium, neon, argon): unreactive gases with full outer shells. Metals conduct heat and electricity, are malleable and ductile and tend to lose electrons; nonmetals are poor conductors and tend to gain electrons. Metalloids such as silicon are semiconductors.
